clinical_category: Total joint arthroplasty - VTE chemoprophylaxis teaching
blueprint_topic: Antithrombotic medication teaching within postoperative VTE prevention
stem: After total knee replacement, a client is prescribed an anticoagulant as part of the postoperative venous thromboembolism prevention plan. Which explanation by the nurse is most accurate?

options.A: Hip and knee arthroplasty carry important postoperative DVT and pulmonary-embolism risk, so the prescribed anticoagulant is one part of an individualized prevention plan that may also include early movement and mechanical measures.
options.B: Lower-extremity joint replacement carries little VTE risk, so the anticoagulant is being used mainly to improve surgical-wound healing.
options.C: Once an anticoagulant is prescribed, ankle movement, mobilization, compression measures, and assessment for clot symptoms are unnecessary.
options.D: The same anticoagulant regimen is required for every joint-replacement client regardless of bleeding risk, clotting history, or other clinical factors.

rationale: A is correct. AAOS identifies blood clots in the leg veins as an important complication after total knee replacement and notes that pulmonary embolism can be life-threatening. AAOS prevention programs may include blood-thinning medication, early foot and ankle movement, compression devices or stockings, and clinical assessment. Current AAOS discussion also emphasizes risk stratification because the choice of chemoprophylaxis is not one-size-fits-all and must balance VTE risk against bleeding and wound risks. B incorrectly minimizes postoperative VTE risk and assigns an unsupported wound-healing purpose to anticoagulation. C is incorrect because pharmacologic prophylaxis does not replace mobility, mechanical prevention, or surveillance. D is incorrect because the prophylactic agent and strategy are individualized. The final item therefore supports the prescribed anticoagulant's role without claiming that one drug or regimen is universally required for every arthroplasty patient.
educational_objective: Explain that prescribed anticoagulant prophylaxis after total joint arthroplasty is used to reduce postoperative VTE risk as one component of an individualized prevention plan that also includes appropriate mobility, mechanical measures, and ongoing assessment.
source_document_title: Total Knee Replacement; Postoperative Risk Factors — Blood Clots and Abnormal Bleeding/Venous Thromboembolism & Anticoagulation; Aspirin for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis after hip and knee arthroplasty is not one-size-fits-all
source_version_date: Current AAOS OrthoInfo and VTE toolkit accessed 2026-08-18; AAOS Now risk-stratification article published 2026-04-25
source_locator: AAOS OrthoInfo 'Total Knee Replacement' → Complications → Blood clots: leg-vein clots are an important complication and can cause life-threatening PE; Hospital Stay → Blood Clot Prevention: blood thinners, compression measures and foot/ankle movement may be used. AAOS VTE Quality Toolkit → Postoperative Risk Factors: orthopaedic operations require preoperative risk recognition and planned VTE prophylaxis. AAOS Now 2026 'Aspirin for VTE prophylaxis after hip and knee arthroplasty is not one-size-fits-all' → Practical takeaways: chemoprophylaxis should be risk-stratified and combined with early mobilization/mechanical prophylaxis rather than applied as one universal regimen.
source_claim_supported: Current AAOS sources directly support clinically important postoperative VTE risk after total knee arthroplasty, use of blood-thinning medication as one prevention measure, complementary mobility/mechanical measures, and individualized risk-stratified prophylaxis rather than a universal anticoagulant regimen.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity → Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, printed p. 12 (PDF pageno 15): educate clients about medications, administer medications safely, review pertinent medication data and evaluate client response to medication.
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source's overbroad 'anticoagulant prophylaxis is standard' statement into individualized postoperative medication teaching. The final item preserves the high VTE-risk rationale while explicitly preventing a one-drug/one-regimen-for-all interpretation and incorporating complementary mechanical and mobility measures supported by AAOS.
audit_findings: The original item correctly recognized VTE risk after major lower-extremity orthopaedic surgery but overstated anticoagulant prophylaxis as a uniform standard without risk stratification.
Fresh AAOS review confirms important DVT/PE risk after total knee replacement and supports blood thinners, mobility and mechanical measures within prevention programs.
Current 2026 AAOS discussion explicitly emphasizes that chemoprophylaxis is not one-size-fits-all and should reflect clotting and bleeding risks.
Distractors test VTE-risk minimization, abandonment of nonpharmacologic measures and universal-regimen overreach; none is defensible.
